title: Behind SteamScope
subtitle: From messy game data to a connected discovery platform

slides.title: Good discovery starts with good data.
slides.lead: A player asks: I loved this game. What should I play next? Our database connects the clues needed to answer.
points: Know the game
Store its name, genres, tags, developers, and recorded popularity.
Know the collection
Keep each demo profile's library, wishlist, and favorites.
Connect the two
Use shared attributes to suggest unowned games and explain the match.
slides.takeaway: The interface is the visible result. The database does the connecting.
slides.notes: Open with the gaming motivation. Then explain that the review will follow the data, not just tour screens.

slides.title: The first challenge was trust.
slides.lead: The original CSV had values under the wrong headings. Importing it directly would have created convincing-looking but incorrect answers.
points: An early warning
The initial sample showed a game description as a number and a review score as a boolean.
A better source
We switched to the clean JSON version, where fields have explicit names and lists keep their structure.
An honest boundary
The corruption observations come from earlier profiling notes. The JSON counts shown here were remeasured for this presentation.
slides.takeaway: We recovered the catalog from JSON; we did not guess how to repair every damaged CSV row.
slides.notes: Do not quote an unverified corruption percentage. Distinguish the historical sample findings from the newly checked JSON file.

slides.title: A small set of careful steps.
slides.lead: We read the large JSON a little at a time, checked each game, and produced consistent files for MySQL.
points: Read in small pieces
The cleaner uses ijson to stream the file instead of loading the entire document at once.
Keep useful records
Trim text, turn blank values into missing values, check IDs, and skip records without names.
Load in the right order
Load games and reference names first. Then create the links between them in batches of 2,000.
slides.takeaway: 141,900 source records - 1 unnamed record = 141,899 retained games.
slides.notes: The original JSON pass found zero duplicate IDs and zero invalid IDs. Duplicate checks exist even though they removed no records in this pass.

slides.title: Clean values, without inventing facts.
slides.lead: Each change makes a value easier to use while keeping its meaning clear.
points: Text
Extra spaces are removed. Blank text becomes missing, rather than a made-up value.
Numbers and dates
The loader converts readable values into database types. A date it cannot understand becomes missing.
Lists
Genres and developers become individual relationships. Tags use the names in the JSON tag dictionary.
slides.takeaway: Unknown is different from zero. A missing price should not automatically mean a free game.
slides.notes: Use the example selector. Date parsing also accepts month/year inputs, which Python interprets as the first day of the month; that is a precision limitation.

slides.title: Store a fact once. Connect it many times.
slides.lead: A game can have several genres, and a genre can describe many games. A separate linking table represents that relationship clearly.
points: Game
One row identifies a game with its Steam app_id.
Genre
One row identifies each genre name, such as Action.
Game + genre
Each linking row says that one game belongs to one genre. The pair of IDs cannot be repeated.
slides.takeaway: This is normalization: separate facts by their purpose, then connect them using IDs.
slides.notes: The diagram is a simple example using two real source titles. Displayed example IDs are labels, not a claim about live genre IDs.

slides.title: 24 tables. Five clear responsibilities.
slides.lead: The final structure separates game facts, reusable names, relationships, media, and the simulated player layer.
points: Catalog and reference names
game plus seven lookup tables: developer, publisher, genre, tag, category, platform, and language.
Connections and media
Seven game-to-attribute tables, plus screenshots and reviews.
Profiles and their history
user, library, wishlist, purchase, achievement, user_achievement, and user_activity.
slides.takeaway: Real catalog data and simulated player data meet through the same game ID.
slides.notes: Counts are saved snapshot results. Some tables may be empty; having a table is not proof that it is populated.
sources: Live database: information_schema and exact table counts

slides.title: One game, many connections.
slides.lead: Follow the lines from game to its attributes. Select a table to inspect its real columns and key fields.
points: 1 to many
One game can appear in many linking rows. Each linking row points to one existing game.
Many to many
A linking table connects many games with many genres, developers, or tags.
Language has an extra detail
support_type distinguishes supported text from full audio. Read the table inspector for the exact key used by this database.
slides.takeaway: PK means a row's unique identity. FK means an ID that points to a row in another table.
slides.notes: This diagram and the next cover all 24 tables. game appears in both. Lines show actual foreign keys; a parent may have zero or many child rows.

slides.title: The game is the common link.
slides.lead: Libraries, wishlists, purchases, and activity connect a profile to a game. Achievements use a separate unlock relationship.
points: Collections
library and wishlist use the profile ID and game ID together as their identity.
Favorites
is_favorite belongs to a library row. A favorite therefore has to be owned.
History
Purchases and activity can contain multiple events for the same profile and game. They need their own event IDs.
slides.takeaway: Public review authors are external Steam IDs; they are not the simulated user table.
slides.notes: There is no review-to-user foreign key. Achievements and activity point to existing entities, but the schema alone does not require their game to be in the current library.
sources: Live database: library, wishlist, purchase, achievement, user_achievement, user_activity

slides.title: Rules that protect the connections.
slides.lead: We checked the saved database, not only the design document. Every declared foreign-key relationship was checked for missing parent rows.
points: Unique identities
Primary keys stop duplicate identities. Composite keys stop repeated collection memberships.
Valid references
Foreign keys stop a linking row from pointing to a game or profile that does not exist.
Know what the checks mean
Zero orphan rows means the declared links are intact. It does not prove every price, date, or recommendation is correct.
slides.takeaway: Integrity checks measure specific properties. They do not make imperfect source data perfect.
slides.notes: Show the actual orphan total and check count. Missing prices and dates are reported rather than silently turned into zero.

slides.title: A useful answer comes from a few connected tables.
slides.lead: Choose a question to see the SQL and its saved result. These results are snapshots, so the presentation works without MySQL running.
points: Connect
JOIN combines related rows using their IDs.
Group
GROUP BY puts rows about the same game or genre together.
Count and order
COUNT measures the group. ORDER BY places the largest results first.
slides.takeaway: The same relationships that organize the data also power rankings and analytics.
slides.notes: Ownership comes from demo libraries, not real Steam owners. Genre counts overlap because a game can have multiple genres.

slides.title: Recommendations you can explain.
slides.lead: Games receive points for shared tags, genres, and developers. Favorite source games contribute three times as much.
points: Shared tag: 3 points
Tags capture clues such as FPS or Multiplayer.
Shared genre: 1 point; developer: 2
Broad categories and the people behind a game add more clues.
Rank the candidates
Exclude owned games, rank by score, and use positive reviews to break ties. Empty profiles get a labeled popularity fallback.
slides.takeaway: This is a transparent rule-based score, not a trained machine-learning model.
slides.notes: The calculator is an illustrative single-source example. The real query adds contributions from all owned source games and aggregates relationship types separately to avoid inflated joins.

slides.title: Add to library. Leave the wishlist.
slides.lead: These two changes should succeed together. If something fails, neither change should be left half-finished.
points: Start
The demo begins with a game on a wishlist.
Make both changes
Add the library row and remove the wishlist row within one database transaction.
Finish or undo
Commit keeps both changes. Rollback returns to the starting state after an error.
slides.takeaway: A transaction is an all-or-nothing promise for related changes.
slides.notes: This is a visual simulation; it never edits the database. The real endpoint locks the profile during collection edits and the shared cursor helper commits or rolls back.

slides.title: Each layer has one clear job.
slides.lead: The browser asks for data. The API checks the request. SQL reads or changes the database. A structured response returns to the screen.
points: React + Vite + CSS
The interface: discovery, collections, recommendations, rankings, and presentation.
Python + FastAPI + Pydantic
The API: routes, request checks, and consistent response shapes. Uvicorn runs it.
MySQL + Connector/Python
Storage and SQL: keys, relationships, joins, counts, pooled connections, and transactions.
slides.takeaway: We use parameterized raw SQL, not an ORM. Python and ijson handle JSON recovery; pandas supports earlier profiling.
slides.notes: Explain technologies by their jobs. Seven integration tests passed during the preceding implementation, including rollback, recommendation scoring, and concurrent reads.

slides.title: A clean structure makes new features possible.
slides.lead: SteamScope turns a recovered game catalog into a connected system that can answer questions and support a working user experience.
points: Delivered
A verified catalog, a 24-table relational structure, demo collections, explainable recommendations, and SQL analytics.
Be clear about limits
Profiles and activity are simulated. Catalog metrics are snapshots. Missing or stale source values still exist.
Next
Package a repeatable database setup, improve recommendation relevance, and later consider new data sources and real authentication.
slides.takeaway: The database is the foundation; the app shows what that foundation makes possible.
slides.notes: Suggested live handoff: show a game, its genres, a demo library, and a recommendation reason. Keep this saved presentation and the PDF available as backup.

slides.title: A story you can trace back to the work.
slides.lead: The presentation uses saved source counts and a read-only database snapshot. Earlier documents are treated as history when they differ from the current schema.
points: Source recovery
JSON recovery, relationship extraction, and database loaders are together in scripts/.
Database evidence
presentation_snapshot.py records columns, keys, table counts, missing values, orphan checks, and two query results.
Application evidence
Collection transactions, recommendation SQL, typed responses, and integration tests live under backend/.
slides.takeaway: Snapshot counts can change after collection edits. No private profile records are embedded in this presentation.
slides.notes: The code path references are local project evidence, not public dataset citations. Exact original dataset download attribution still needs to be added before external distribution.
